newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka tea exporters go for own brands.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka tea exporters go for own brands.

text.p: Sri Lankan tea exporters should establish their own brands in sophisticated Western markets to develop the island's main commodity export, a leading gourmet tea exporter said on Sunday.
"Everybody here must try and establish their own brands for the West," Anselm Perera, managing director of Euro-Scan Exports, said in an interview.
"We should be almost 100 percent in packeted teas. The sale of loose tea ... will become smaller and smaller because people are getting busier and busier," he said.
"People have no time to brew tea, so they go more for products like tea bags, instant tea."

Sri Lanka, the world's leading tea exporter, still exports most of its tea in bulk as it has done for over a 100 years, but exporters are gradually realising the importance of selling value-added products, Perera said.

Exports of Ceylon tea remain the island's main net foreign exchange earner and about half of total tea export earnings of 24 billion rupees ($421 million) last year came from value-added teas, industry officials said.
Sri Lanka, whose tea exports are expected to hit a record 250 million kg this calendar year, satisfies about 20 percent of world demand.
Tea industry officials said more than 10 companies were now exporting packeted teas, with a few like Euro-Scan targeting the high end of the market.
Euro-Scan sells 1,500 different types of tea products, ranging from tea bags to metal cans, reed baskets, leather packs, porcelain containers and gift tea packs, in 38 markets.
"We have the widest range of tea packets -- 1,500 items -- in the world," Perera said.
"We spend a lot of money and effort on design. The first five years on my own were very tough. I realised that if we didn't go with a really class product we can't sell.
"To get the younger generation we went for a large variety of flavoured tea," he added.
The company exports 80 percent of its tea in packeted form, up from 25 percent when it was set up in 1983, he said.
Tea expert Maxwell Fernando, author of a new book on trading in Ceylon tea, said value-added consumer products like tea packets, bags, instant tea, and herbal and scented teas earn than bulk tea.
Exports of value-added teas from Sri Lanka rose sharply last year mainly because of heavy Russian buying which sent prices to record levels.
"My biggest single market was Japan," Perera said. "Then it became the United States and Canada and now it is Russia."
Russia and other members of the Commonwealth of Independent States bought 40.4 million kg of Sri Lankan tea last year, the bulk of it in packets, brokers Forbes and Walker said.
This was up 206 percent from a year earlier.
Value-added tea accounted for 43 percent of total tea exports of 235 million kg last year from 32 percent in 1994.
